strengths: The paper targets a relevant and important failure mode of VLMs: reliance on memorized priors over visual evidence in objective visual tasks.

It provides a broad empirical study across seven domains (animals, logos, flags, chess/xiangqi, board games, optical illusions, patterned grids), multiple SOTA VLMs, three image resolutions, and multiple question types.
The benchmark includes sanity checks on unmodified images, showing 100% recognition for a subset, and analyzes bias-aligned errors rather than only aggregate accuracy.

The paper tests in-image textual cues and helpful prompting strategies, finding that debiasing/double-check prompts yield only modest improvements and that adding subject-name text further degrades counterfactual accuracy.
The automated generation pipeline combining LLMs, image editors, and scripts is promising for scalable counterfactual benchmark construction, with human review for quality control.
Qualitative examples illustrate striking failures, e.g., counting stripes on modified Adidas-like logos and legs on modified animals, which may be useful for the community.
weaknesses: The central claim that low accuracy is due to Internet-derived bias is not cleanly isolated from VLMs' general inability to count or visually inspect details. The patterned-grid task, which has no memorized web prior, also yields very low accuracy (22.44%) and pattern-aligned errors, suggesting that visual counting/Gestalt limitations substantially contribute to the reported failures.

The sanity check is narrow: only 66 unmodified images are used to claim 100% recognition across tasks, not the full original sets. More importantly, there is no human baseline or matched control task with non-famous objects of similar visual complexity, so the 17.05% counterfactual accuracy cannot be conclusively attributed to knowledge bias rather than counting difficulty.

The in-image text experiment is confounded: inserting subject-name text changes image layout, aspect ratio, and OCR load. Without neutral-text, non-subject text, or same-length control conditions, the accuracy drop cannot be uniquely attributed to semantic bias from the text corpus.

Evaluation rigor is limited: only proprietary API models are tested, no repeated runs/variance/confidence intervals are reported despite temperature=1.0, and there are no statistical tests. The benchmark sizes are uneven across tasks, and it is unclear whether Q1 and Q2 are treated as independent samples or averaged per image.

Manual quality control of generated counterfactuals is not quantitatively documented. There is no inter-annotator agreement, no reported rejection rates, and no independent validation that every modified image has exactly the intended number of elements. This is critical because incorrect ground truth would directly produce low accuracy.

Novelty is incremental relative to prior work showing that VLMs hallucinate on counterfactual/visual-dependency benchmarks, rely on language priors, fail at counting, and perform poorly on modified optical illusions. The main new components—counting questions and in-image adversarial text—are useful but may not constitute a sufficiently strong top-tier contribution.

The paper conflates several distinct failure modes: semantic memory bias, low-level visual counting limitations, and Gestalt/pattern-completion biases. Averaging across all seven tasks into a single 17.05% score obscures which mechanisms drive errors and weakens the specificity of the conclusions.

Reproducibility is a concern: the code/data link is blank in the manuscript, proprietary model versions may change, and exact API settings/default behavior are difficult to reproduce. No open-source VLMs are evaluated, limiting generality.

The title and abstract make broad claims ('VLMs are biased') that are stronger than the evidence from specific synthetic counterfactual images and selected subjects. The limitations section is brief and does not adequately address these conceptual, statistical, and reproducibility concerns.
There are formatting/typographical issues throughout (e.g., 'Adadias', 'Nonnet-3.7', 'chese', 'Sodomu', 'Pyllusion', inconsistent citations), which reduce clarity and polish for a top-tier venue.

strengths: The paper targets a timely and important failure mode: visual prior/knowledge bias in VLMs, moving beyond social bias and biased textual prompts to objective counting questions.

It constructs a relatively diverse benchmark across 7 domains (animals, logos, flags, chess, game boards, optical illusions, patterned grids) with 1,392 counterfactual images, multiple resolutions, and sanity-check, in-image-text, debiasing, and double-check experiments.

The empirical results are striking and consistent across five SOTA VLMs: near-100% accuracy on unmodified images but about 17% on counterfactual counting, with a high proportion of bias-aligned errors.
The paper evaluates both thinking and non-thinking models and shows that larger reasoning effort or standard debiasing prompts do not solve the issue, which is a useful negative result.
weaknesses: The central claim that failures are caused by “bias” from memorized prior knowledge is not causally isolated. Alternative explanations include general VLM blindness to fine-grained counting, yes/no response bias, prompt sensitivity, and low-quality or ambiguous counterfactual edits. The patterned-grid task, where no prior knowledge exists, further undermines the broad bias interpretation.

There is no human baseline or human evaluation of image quality. Since many failures involve subtle visual changes, it is unclear whether VLMs are making bias-driven errors or simply failing at difficult low-level counting/perception tasks that humans would also struggle with, especially for small logos, faint legs, and striped flags.

No repeated sampling, confidence intervals, or statistical tests are reported. Results are often single-run comparisons at temperature 1.0, making small reported differences (e.g., +2 points from debiasing) unreliable.

The counterfactual image generation pipeline relies on text-to-image models and an unspecified manual filtering process. The paper does not quantify rejected images, inter-annotator agreement, or residual artifacts, and some evaluated models (Gemini, GPT-4.1) are from the same families as the image generators, potentially confounding original-image recognition.

Novelty is limited relative to prior work on VLM blindness, hallucination, and visual counterfactual benchmarks. The main new ingredient—neutral counting questions instead of biased yes/no prompts—is useful but incremental, and the paper does not provide deeper mechanistic analysis of vision encoder vs. language prior.

Evaluation is narrow: only proprietary API models are tested, with no open-source VLMs, non-VLM vision baselines, or controlled ablations that remove language priors. The causal claim about the text corpus remains speculative.

The debiasing study is weak: only two generic prompts are tested, with no exploration of stronger interventions, and the negative result is used to support a strong conclusion about VLMs being irredeemably biased.

The benchmark conflates multiple constructs—knowledge bias, counting ability, pattern inference, and low-level visual perception—under a single “bias” label. This makes it difficult to interpret what exactly has been measured and which conclusions are supported.

Reproducibility is incomplete: code/data URLs are missing or redacted in the manuscript, exact API versions and parsing/validation details are underspecified, and there are many typos and nomenclature inconsistencies that reduce clarity.

strengths: Introduces VLM Bias, an automated benchmark of 1,392 counterfactual images across seven domains with neutral counting/identification questions, multiple resolutions, and optional in-image adversarial text.

Comprehensive evaluation of five SOTA VLMs, including thinking and non-thinking models, with an original-image sanity check where all models achieve 100% accuracy before failing on counterfactual versions.

Clear empirical findings: mean counting accuracy on counterfactual images is 17.05%, about 75% of errors align with memorized biases, and helpful prompts such as debiasing or double-checking improve accuracy only modestly (+1.87 to +2.70 points).

Strong positioning relative to prior benchmarks: unlike PhD, VLind-Bench, and HallusionBench, the work uses neutral prompts, objective counting tasks, automated counterfactual generation, and in-image textual bias injection.
Well-structured presentation, qualitative examples, error analysis, released code/data, and acknowledged limitations; findings are consistent across many tasks and model families.
weaknesses: The central claim that VLMs are biased is not fully disentangled from low-level visual counting or acuity limitations. The original-image sanity check can be solved via prior knowledge, and no non-famous control objects with identical counterfactual modifications are provided to isolate semantic bias from perceptual failure.

Counterfactual image quality and perceptibility are not rigorously validated. Some modifications, especially small car logos, may be hard to see at the tested resolutions; human accuracy or vision-encoder probing is missing.

Evaluation is limited to proprietary API models with default settings, likely a single run per condition, and no confidence intervals or variance estimates, which weakens reproducibility and statistical strength.

Mechanistic evidence for the proposed bias account is limited. The paper suggests future work comparing vision encoder representations, but does not show whether the modified visual detail is represented internally and then overridden by language priors.

Prompt-based mitigation yields only small gains, and the paper remains primarily diagnostic without proposing a robust solution; some results on novel patterned grids also support general visual counting difficulty as an alternative explanation.

strengths: Introduces a systematic benchmark (VLMBIAS) spanning 7 diverse domains with 1,392 counterfactual images, neutral prompts, and multiple question types, going beyond prior biased-prompt VQA benchmarks.

Provides extensive empirical evaluation across 5 SOTA VLMs, plus additional open-source, latest, and pointing/counting-specialized models, with controls for resolution, repeated runs, and prompt variations.
Key findings are clear and well supported: VLMs score 100% on original images but only ~17% on counterfactual counting images, defaulting to prior-knowledge answers ~75% of the time.

Additional analyses are informative, including background removal (+21.09 accuracy), in-image adversarial text, few-shot prompting, tool use, thinking-token analysis, and a human study on animal counting.

Linear probing on vision-encoder features suggests the visual encoder encodes sufficient information, supporting the claim that language priors override visual evidence rather than a purely perceptual failure.
Paper is well written, transparent about limitations, and provides code/data for reproducibility; extensive appendix documents task construction and qualitative failures.
weaknesses: Novelty is somewhat limited: prior work already shows VLM bias, language-prior over-reliance, and counting failures; this paper mainly extends such findings to counterfactual counting with neutral prompts and a new benchmark.

Human validation is only performed on the animal leg-counting task, not on logos, flags, chess, game boards, optical illusions, or patterned grids, leaving potential ambiguity or image-generation artifacts in other domains insufficiently validated.

The generated counterfactual images rely on SOTA image editors and manual filtering, but the paper does not report inter-annotator agreement, rejection rates, or detailed quality-control statistics, raising concerns about selection artifacts.

The "bias rate" metric is not equally meaningful across tasks: for binary optical-illusion questions, random guessing already yields ~50% bias alignment, and the metric conflates biased answers with other errors.

Background removal improves accuracy, but it may also simplify the task or remove useful contextual information; the causal claim that background cues trigger bias could be stronger with more controlled ablations.
Thinking-token analysis is observational and may suffer from selection bias: harder examples could induce different reasoning lengths, so the inverted-U relationship is not necessarily causal.
The paper's broad title and claim ("VLMs are biased") are not fully aligned with the narrower scope of prior-knowledge bias in counting/identification on counterfactual images.
No mitigation method is proposed or rigorously evaluated beyond prompt-level interventions and tool use; the work is primarily diagnostic.

strengths: The paper studies a timely and interesting failure mode: state-of-the-art VLMs often default to canonical answers instead of counting modified visual elements in counterfactual images.
It introduces a sizable, diverse benchmark (1,392 main images across animals, logos, flags, chess, board games, optical illusions, and patterned grids) with automated generation plus human review.

Several analyses go beyond a simple benchmark: sanity checks, background removal, linear probing of the vision encoder, in-image text injection, repeated runs, human study, and thinking-token/tool-use analyses.
The sanity-check experiments suggest that models recognize the original popular subjects and can answer their canonical counts, which helps motivate the counterfactual evaluation.
The paper is generally transparent about generation prompts, model settings, and experimental procedures, and it attempts to release code/data and report reproducibility details.
Findings such as the effect of background removal and bias toward internal grid patterns could be useful for future VLM evaluation and mitigation work.
weaknesses: The central claim that VLMs are 'biased' is stronger than the evidence. Low accuracy on these tasks could reflect poor fine-grained counting/perception, not necessarily language-prior bias. The paper needs stronger controls to separate visual counting difficulty from prior-knowledge override.

The 'bias rate' metric is not clean: an incorrect answer that happens to match a pre-defined canonical count is counted as bias, but models may produce that number for other reasons. Chance levels and alternative baselines are mostly missing for counting tasks.

The background-removal experiment is confounded. Removing backgrounds or regenerating images for abstract domains may alter task difficulty, remove essential context, or change the visual question itself. Aggregating heterogeneous transformations into a +21.09 accuracy claim overstates what is isolated.

The reasoning-token analysis is correlational rather than causal. 'Overthinking harms accuracy' is not demonstrated by controlled manipulation; harder questions naturally require more tokens and may have lower accuracy.

Some results are reported inconsistently. For example, the optical-illusion discussion conflates original-image accuracy (78.02%) with bias rate, and Table 2's 'Unmodified Task mean = 100.00' excludes some tasks while being presented as a general sanity check.

Evaluation lacks important baselines: no simple visual counting baseline (e.g., detector plus counter), no no-prior control with non-famous or novel subjects of similar counting difficulty, and no direct comparison against closest prior benchmarks in the main experiments.

The human study is limited to the animal task and time-limited viewing. It does not establish that counterfactuals in logos, flags, chess, boards, and patterned grids are unambiguous or human-solvable.

The novelty is incremental. Prior work already documents VLM language priors, hallucination, and counting failures. The shift to neutral prompts and counting is useful, but the paper does not fully distinguish itself from existing findings.
The presentation is dense and sometimes unclear, with typographical errors, inconsistent model names/icons, unclear table columns, and a missing code/data URL in the abstract.

Several tasks may be extremely hard for non-specialized models even without any language bias (e.g., counting rows in modified Go/Sudoku/chess boards), making it difficult to attribute failures primarily to bias rather than basic visual counting limitations.

strengths: Introduces VLMBias, a systematic counterfactual benchmark across seven diverse domains with neutral prompts and objective counting/identification questions, addressing key limitations of prior VLM bias benchmarks that rely on biased prompts or Y/N questions.

Extensive evaluation spans multiple SOTA VLMs (closed and open-source), includes sanity checks, background removal, in-image text injection, helpful prompting, few-shot prompting, tool use, latest models, and pointing VLMs, making the empirical study broad and informative.

Provides mechanistic evidence via linear probing that the vision encoder contains sufficient information to distinguish counterfactual leg counts while the full VLM fails, supporting the hypothesis that language priors override visual evidence.

Interesting and actionable findings: background removal substantially improves counting accuracy and reduces bias, thinking-token analysis reveals an empirical accuracy ceiling, and small pointing VLMs substantially outperform much larger commercial VLMs.
Includes a human study showing that the counterfactual images are not inherently ambiguous and that humans, given sufficient viewing time, can solve the tasks at high accuracy.
weaknesses: The central claim that failures are due to bias is partially confounded with task difficulty and possible out-of-distribution artifacts from generated/edited counterfactual images; background removal may make counting easier independently of bias, and the linear-probing evidence covers only one model and one domain.

Benchmark construction relies on SOTA image generators/editors with manual filtering, which may introduce artifacts or selection biases; the 100% sanity-check accuracy on original images may reflect memorized prior knowledge rather than genuine visual recognition.

The evaluation generally lacks statistical significance tests, confidence intervals, or detailed variance reporting across most tasks; several tasks have relatively few images, and the human study is limited to the animal domain.

Novelty is moderate: prior work already shows VLMs can rely on language priors or fail on counterfactual images, and this paper mainly provides a more systematic counting-focused benchmark and analyses rather than a new method or mitigation.

Some claims and framing are stronger than the evidence supports (e.g., that background visual cues 'trigger biased responses' or the broad title 'Vision Language Models are Biased'), and the main paper is somewhat cluttered with many figures/tables that could be streamlined.
